::: {#fig-10-intent-lease-envelope fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Localization uncertainty and authority expiry**: Panel (a) draws the handle estimate's 95 percent region to scale against the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance: the lateral semi-axis of `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_x_str` fits, while the `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_z_str` depth semi-axis along the camera ray does not. Panel (b) sketches speed against time: renewals keep the lease alive, and when they stop the lease expires, the drive takes `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_arm_onset_str` to begin braking, and a jerk-limited stop follows. The shaded area is the stopping distance, which must fit the clearance that remains; the dashed trace is motion with no lease, which never stops." fig-alt="Two panels. Left: a tall ellipse labeled 95 percent region, centered on point p0 below a wrist camera, overlaps a dashed square labeled tolerance 15 millimeters; the ellipse fits the square sideways, with a lateral dimension of 11.2 millimeters, but extends above and below it, with a depth dimension of 33.5 millimeters. Right: speed against time. A solid line at v max carries three renewal dots, then a red vertical line marks lease expiry, an amber band marks drive onset 22 milliseconds, and the line curves smoothly down to zero speed. The area under the falling part is shaded and labeled d stop equals the integral of v dt, at most the clearance left. A red dashed line continues at v max, labeled no lease, no stop. Brackets under the axis mark the admitted lease and the jerk-limited stop."}
![](images/svg/fig10_intent_lease_envelope.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The two traces in @fig-10-intent-lease-envelope are alternative outcomes. Fresh measurements can support continued tracking; a missed renewal invokes the validated stop. Neither outcome repairs the distant view's excessive depth uncertainty, and stopping before the obstacle still depends on the complete response budget.

A detection with a large uncertainty estimate can be rejected by a configured statistical gate. A confident grounding to the wrong physical entity can pass that gate. Suppose instead that a thin-walled glass jar arrives alone where the mug should be, and the vision-language model assigns it a high confidence score when asked for the red mug. The model emits a sharp, low-variance geometric proposal centered on the glass. The trajectory planner receives the coordinate, computes an $SE(3)$ inverse kinematics solution, verifies joint limits, and confirms that the path clears all obstacles in the static environment map. The permission path may find the proposed motion within its configured geometric and force bounds. If those bounds allow the grip force the ceramic mug needs, a smooth, geometrically valid trajectory can crush the glass despite passing the checks.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_wrong_object_chain.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three dots joined by arrows: an orange dot labeled confident wrong object, a slate dot labeled passes geometric checks, and a red dot labeled mug-rated squeeze."}

*A confident wrong object passes every geometric check until the gripper closes.*
:::

This failure reveals the boundary between what the permission path can verify and what it must accept as an unvalidated premise. The permission path checks coordinate bounds, kinematic reachability, joint torque limits, and geometric collisions against known occupancy grids. Those physical checks do not establish that the coordinate names the intended object, so the premise that the grasped object is the named object lies outside the permission path's reach. It needs its own task evidence, and it travels with the mug into the handover branch of the release case (@sec-release-case-worked-full) and into the register of claims the machine's evidence leaves open (@sec-frontier-residual-claims-register).

Multimodal feature extraction, cross-attention alignment, and open-vocabulary phrase grounding belong to the computer vision and language literature [@kamath2021mdetr; @gu2022open; @radford2021learning; @liu2023grounding]. A physical AI architecture consumes these grounding models without relying on their internal activations for safety, and even a filtered proposal stream still needs the independent motion-permission check. AutoRT's language-model task filter raised the fraction of acceptable proposed tasks but let some unsuitable ones through, and the teleoperators supervising data collection, not the filter, stopped them (\ref{ws-intent-autort-hallucination-constitution}) [@ahn2023autort].

```{python}
#| label: calc-intent-autort-filter
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
# │ AutoRT task-filter counts (Ahn et al. 2024, Sec. 5.3): acceptable fractions │
# │ before and after the constitutional filter, and the filter's recall.        │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
# ┌── 1. LOAD: reported counts ────────────────────────────────────────────────
n_total = 259  # category: literature (Ahn et al. 2024, tasks sampled)
n_ok = 228  # category: literature (acceptable before filtering)
n_kept = 214  # category: literature (kept by the filter)
n_kept_ok = 200  # category: literature (acceptable among kept)
n_bad = 31  # category: literature (unsuitable tasks in the sample)
n_caught = 17  # category: literature (unsuitable tasks the filter rejected)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: fractions and recall ────────────────────────────────────────
n_missed = n_bad - n_caught
pct_before = 100 * n_ok / n_total
pct_after = 100 * n_kept_ok / n_kept
recall = 100 * n_caught / n_bad

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(n_total - n_ok == n_bad, "Unsuitable count matches the sample")
check(n_kept - n_kept_ok == n_missed, "Unsuitable tasks the filter kept match the misses")
check(round(pct_before) == 88 and round(pct_after) == 93 and round(recall) == 55, "Reported percentages")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class AutoRTFilter:
    n_total_str = fmt_int(n_total)
    n_ok_str = fmt_int(n_ok)
    n_kept_str = fmt_int(n_kept)
    n_kept_ok_str = fmt_int(n_kept_ok)
    n_bad_str = fmt_int(n_bad)
    n_caught_str = fmt_int(n_caught)
    n_missed_str = fmt_int(n_missed)
    pct_before_str = fmt_int(round(pct_before))
    pct_after_str = fmt_int(round(pct_after))
    recall_str = fmt_int(round(recall))
```

::: {#ws-intent-autort-hallucination-constitution .callout-war-story title="AutoRT task filtering and supervision (2024)"}
**Context**: AutoRT deployed foundation models to propose and filter physical manipulation tasks for fleets of mobile manipulators operating in unstructured human office environments [@ahn2023autort].

**Mechanism**: In a sample of `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_total_str` proposed tasks, human annotators judged `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_ok_str` (`{python} AutoRTFilter.pct_before_str` percent) acceptable. A second LLM pass then filtered the tasks against a robot "constitution" of safety and embodiment rules. Of the `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_kept_str` tasks it kept, `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_kept_ok_str` (`{python} AutoRTFilter.pct_after_str` percent) were acceptable. The filter rejected `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_caught_str` of the `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_bad_str` unsuitable tasks, a recall of `{python} AutoRTFilter.recall_str` percent, and passed the other `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_missed_str`.

**Impact**: All `{python} AutoRTFilter.n_missed_str` misses arose during teleoperated collection, and the teleoperator rejected each one before the robot acted on it. The filter improved the proposal stream; the human supervisor, not the filter, stopped every unsuitable task that reached a robot.

**Response**: The system architecture placed physical safety outside the model's domain: deployments supplemented learned proposals with hardware joint-force limits, physical emergency stop buttons, and direct human line-of-sight supervision or physical perimeter barricades.

**Systems lesson**: A learned task filter can improve proposal quality, but it cannot serve as a safety referee. An independent, deterministic permission and fallback path must validate every physical action against real-time plant limits before execution.
:::

Once the mug candidate has a metric frame and a dated record, alternative proposal sources can use the same interface. The sources in @tbl-10-grounding-paradigms differ in what they make available to the planner. SayCan ranks pretrained skills using semantic relevance and learned value [@ahn2022saycan]; Code as Policies generates scripts that call perception and control interfaces [@liang2023code]. VoxPoser supplies spatial value maps (@fig-10-value-map-composition), while OK-Robot selects candidate grasps (@fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding). Each can help turn a request into a useful action candidate, but its output still needs current geometric, effort, and timing checks.

Predicting a plausible coordinate or motion script does not establish physical feasibility. A language or action model is trained to make its outputs likely under its training data, and nothing in that objective represents metric distance, rigid-body non-penetration, the arm's Jacobian, or friction. Each of those needs an independent check in a stated frame: a signed-distance query over the robot geometry for clearance, an inverse-kinematics solve with joint-limit and conditioning screens (@sec-appendix-control-kinematics), and a contact model for the wrench the grasp must carry. Contact-rich or non-prehensile proposals, such as sliding, unlatching, or a handover, can also be rolled out in a physics simulator before the arm commits energy, and the verdict is only as good as the simulated geometry, friction, and dynamics. Such checks identify physically plausible interactions for the planner; they do not replace admission of the resulting motion.

::: {#fig-10-value-map-composition fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Composing value maps for a grasp request**: An original schematic of the value-map interface introduced by VoxPoser [@huang2023voxposer], drawn on one horizontal slice of a voxel grid. (a) An affordance map rewards voxels near the handle the instruction names. (b) An avoidance map penalizes voxels near an observed obstacle. (c) The planner searches the composed cost for a path. The path is good only with respect to the maps: an obstacle the observations missed adds nothing to the avoidance map, so the path can run through it." fig-alt="Three heat maps of the same rectangular grid. Left: green shading, darkest around a star marking the handle. Middle: red shading, darkest around a small square marking an observed obstacle. Right: gray composed cost with a bronze path that runs from a dot on the left, arches over the dark obstacle region, and ends at the star, passing through a hollow red square labeled unobserved obstacle."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-intent-value-map-composition
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ VALUE-MAP COMPOSITION FOR A GRASP REQUEST (SCHEMATIC FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-10-value-map-composition
# │
# │ Goal:    teach the value-map interface (affordance + avoidance -> cost ->
# │          planner) and its blind spot, in an original drawing.
# │ Show:    three maps on one voxel slice and the planned path, which passes
# │          through an obstacle the observations missed.
# │ How:     schematic fields on a unitless grid; Dijkstra on the composed cost.
# │          No physical quantity is drawn.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import heapq
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz

# ┌── 1. LOAD: a schematic tabletop slice (no physical claim) ───────────────
NX, NY = 60, 36  # voxel columns and rows in the drawn slice  # category: illustrative (drawing)
START = (4, 18)  # gripper voxel  # category: illustrative (drawing)
TARGET = (52, 22)  # handle voxel named by the instruction  # category: illustrative (drawing)
OBSTACLE = (30, 17)  # voxel center of an observed obstacle  # category: illustrative (drawing)
SIGMA_OBS = 5.0  # voxels, avoidance falloff  # category: illustrative (drawing)
W_AVOID = 12.0  # weight of avoidance against affordance  # category: illustrative (drawing)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: compose value maps, then plan on the composed cost ─────────
yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:NY, 0:NX]
dist_t = np.hypot(xx - TARGET[0], yy - TARGET[1])
affordance = np.exp(-dist_t / 18.0)  # high near the handle
avoidance = np.exp(-((xx - OBSTACLE[0]) ** 2 + (yy - OBSTACLE[1]) ** 2) / (2 * SIGMA_OBS**2))
cost = (1.0 - affordance) + W_AVOID * avoidance + 0.05

def _plan(c, s, g):
    """Dijkstra over 8-connected voxels; returns the voxel path from s to g."""
    best = {s: 0.0}
    prev = {}
    pq = [(0.0, s)]
    while pq:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if u == g:
            break
        if d > best.get(u, np.inf):
            continue
        for dx in (-1, 0, 1):
            for dy in (-1, 0, 1):
                v = (u[0] + dx, u[1] + dy)
                if (dx or dy) and 0 <= v[0] < NX and 0 <= v[1] < NY:
                    nd = d + np.hypot(dx, dy) * c[v[1], v[0]]
                    if nd < best.get(v, np.inf):
                        best[v] = nd
                        prev[v] = u
                        heapq.heappush(pq, (nd, v))
    path = [g]
    while path[-1] != s:
        path.append(prev[path[-1]])
    return np.array(path[::-1])

path = _plan(cost, START, TARGET)
UNSEEN = tuple(path[int(0.72 * len(path))])  # an obstacle the observations missed lies on the path

# ┌── 3. PLOT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
viz.set_book_style()
C = viz.COLORS
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.6, 2.05))
panels = (
    (affordance, "Greens", "(a) affordance map"),
    (avoidance, "Reds", "(b) avoidance map"),
    (cost, "Greys", "(c) composed cost, planned path"),
)
for ax, (field, cmap, title) in zip(axes, panels):
    ax.imshow(field, origin="lower", cmap=cmap, interpolation="nearest", vmin=0, vmax=np.percentile(field, 99))
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.5, fontweight="normal", pad=4)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.grid(False)
    ax.plot(*TARGET, marker="*", ms=9, color=viz.VOL4_ROLES["structural"], mec="white", mew=0.6, zorder=5)
    ax.plot(*OBSTACLE, marker="s", ms=6, color=viz.VOL4_ROLES["consequence"], mec="white", mew=0.6, zorder=5)
axes[0].text(
    TARGET[0],
    TARGET[1] - 5,
    "handle",
    fontsize=8,
    ha="center",
    va="top",
    color=C["primary"],
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none"),
)
axes[1].text(OBSTACLE[0], OBSTACLE[1] - 8, "observed\nobstacle", fontsize=8, ha="center", va="top", color=C["primary"])
ax = axes[2]
ax.plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], color=viz.VOL4_ROLES["proposal"], lw=1.8, zorder=4)
ax.plot(*START, marker="o", ms=5, color=viz.VOL4_ROLES["proposal"], zorder=5)
ax.plot(*UNSEEN, marker="s", ms=7, mfc="white", mec=viz.VOL4_ROLES["consequence"], mew=1.2, ls="none", zorder=5)
ax.text(UNSEEN[0] - 5, UNSEEN[1] - 3, "unobserved\nobstacle", fontsize=8, ha="right", va="top", color=viz.VOL4_ROLES["consequence"])
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.88, bottom=0.02, wspace=0.06)
plt.show()
```

:::

In @fig-10-value-map-composition, Huang et al. [-@huang2023voxposer] turn instructions such as "open the top drawer" into spatial objectives. Attraction toward a handle and repulsion from observed obstacles guide the optimizer toward a useful interaction. The planner must still check the resulting path and actuator demands; an obstacle missing from the observations also remains missing from the generated field.

::: {#fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Open-vocabulary grasp grounding pipeline**: OK-Robot combines candidate grasp generation with language-conditioned object selection and geometric filtering [@liu2024okrobot]. An open-vocabulary detector isolates the target object mask, candidate grasps are sampled across the 3D point cloud, and geometric heuristics prune inadmissible approaches. The resulting grasp pose represents a candidate proposal; bounding tolerances, evidence deadlines, and independent permission checks are an architectural wrapper developed in this chapter. (Source: Liu et al., 2024 [@liu2024okrobot], CC BY 4.0)." fig-alt="OK-Robot figure showing a robot camera view, candidate grasps, a language-conditioned target mask, filtering, and a selected grasp pose. The image illustrates proposal generation; it does not show a certified collision check or an expiring intent lease."}
![](images/jpg/fig10_real_open_vocab_grounding.jpg){width="95%"}
:::

In @fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding, Liu et al. [-@liu2024okrobot] separate language-conditioned object selection from geometric grasp generation. OWL-ViT finds the object, SAM refines its box into a mask, and AnyGrasp proposes grasps over the whole scene, which the mask then filters to the requested referent. The selected pose still requires dated evidence, effort bounds, and expiry before it can support execution.

| Proposal source           | Representation sent downstream                          | Early check                                                | Remaining evidence needed                                                                              |
|:--------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 2D box or mask            | Image region plus measured depth and camera calibration | Reject absent depth or a target outside a validated region | 3D pose error, occlusion, object identity, and swept-path clearance                                    |
| 3D feature or value field | Candidate target or cost field in a stated frame        | Reject out-of-workspace targets and stale map cells        | Conservative occupancy, unknown-space policy, actuator and timing bounds                               |
| Action VLA                | Decoded action or action chunk in its trained range     | Reject out-of-range or inadmissible proposals              | State-dependent physical limit and independent permission; the action head provides no clearance proof |
| Learned grasp generator   | Set of 6-DoF grasp poses with learned scores            | Reject grasps outside the workspace or jaw aperture        | Measured success on this gripper, IK and joint limits, approach clearance, and wrench capacity         |
| Language-selected skill   | Skill identifier with estimated success                 | Rank or decline low-confidence candidates                  | Current preconditions, path feasibility, and separate physical enforcement                             |

: **Grounding representations and admission questions**: Outputs from different model families require different conversions before a physical permission check. {#tbl-10-grounding-paradigms tbl-colwidths="[18,24,24,34]"}

```{python}
#| label: calc-intent-state-of-practice
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
# │ Literature values quoted beside the state-of-practice table.               │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
# ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
n_action_bins = 256  # category: literature (Brohan et al. 2023, RT-1; Kim et al. 2024, OpenVLA)

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(n_action_bins == 2**8, "Uniform action bins fit one byte per dimension")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
class StateOfPractice:
    n_bins_str = fmt_int(n_action_bins)
```

Whatever the output head, a VLA's action carries no metric bound. Early VLAs such as RT-1 and OpenVLA discretize each action dimension into `{python} StateOfPractice.n_bins_str` uniform bins over its training range [@brohan2023rt1; @kim2024openvla]. FAST compresses an action chunk with a discrete cosine transform before tokenizing it [@pertsch2025fast], and $\pi_0$ replaces tokens with a flow-matching action expert that outputs continuous chunks [@black2024pi0]. In every case the output is a normalized action inside the training distribution, carrying zero metric clearance to obstacles. Location tokens in vision-language models such as PaliGemma quantize normalized image coordinates instead, and they become a metric pose only through measured depth, the calibration chain, and an uncertainty model whose depth and extrinsic terms can easily dominate the quantization grid.

The mechanisms above are durable; the systems that implement them are not. @Tbl-10-state-of-practice names current instances of each role, with what each emits and what the permission path must still establish without it.

| Role in the pipeline                 | Representative systems (year)               | What the system emits                                    | What the permission path must still establish           |
|:-------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| Open-vocabulary detection            | OWL-ViT (2022), Grounding DINO (2023)       | Boxes with independent per-box text scores               | Uniqueness, depth, and object identity                  |
| Promptable segmentation and tracking | SAM 2 (2024)                                | Object masks propagated through video                    | The tracker's own error and latency bounds              |
| Learned grasp generation             | Contact-GraspNet (2021), AnyGrasp (2023)    | Scored 6-DoF grasp sets                                  | IK, aperture, clearance, and wrench capacity            |
| Language to symbolic plan            | LLM+P (2023)                                | A PDDL problem solved by a classical planner             | Every geometric precondition                            |
| Calibrated request for help          | KnowNo (2023)                               | A conformal prediction set over options                  | Coverage under distribution shift; physical singulation |
| VLA action heads                     | OpenVLA (2024), $\pi_0$ (2024), FAST (2025) | Binned tokens, flow-matched chunks, or compressed tokens | Clearance, timing, and effort bounds                    |

: **State of practice for grounded intent, as of 2026**: Representative published systems for each pipeline role [@minderer2022simple; @liu2023grounding; @ravi2024sam2; @sundermeyer2021contactgraspnet; @fang2023anygrasp; @liu2023llmp; @ren2023robots; @kim2024openvla; @black2024pi0; @pertsch2025fast]. The rightmost column is the durable part; later editions should refresh the systems. {#tbl-10-state-of-practice tbl-colwidths="[20,24,26,30]"}

The distant view fails on depth uncertainty, and the wrong-object example fails on a different premise: precise geometry does not establish identity. A useful candidate therefore carries both dated metric evidence and task-specific selection evidence. The handoff must preserve those distinctions while limiting the time and effort available to pursue the target.

## The Intent Handoff and Bounded Authority {#sec-intent-handoff}

When the arm reaches for the red mug, the Brain sends neither joint trajectories nor winding voltages across the proposal boundary. It requests a target region, an expiry, and limits on physical effort. The independent permission path checks those bounds using retained evidence and configured plant limits. Admitting the target allows a planner to seek a motion toward it; it does not admit that motion or give the model access to actuator registers.

The independent permission path evaluates the requested target bounds before the planner relies on them. Host-side geometry work supplies bounded local evidence under a qualified interface; the full scene map does not become MCU-resident merely because a check consumes it. The checks span four mandatory invariants:

1. *Spatial containment invariant:* The proposed geometric goal set $\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}} \subset SE(3)$ must lie strictly within the robot's reachable workspace manifold $\mathcal{W}$, and the bounded spatial uncertainty envelope $(e_x, e_y, e_z)$ must fit inside the task tolerance $(r_x, r_y, r_z)$ without intersecting persistent obstacle geometry in spatial memory $\mathcal{M}$.
2. *Temporal freshness invariant:* The sensor evidence epoch $t_0$ must match a retained parent belief record, and the unobserved elapsed time on the Safety MCU's monotonic hardware clock must not exceed the target-evidence horizon $\tau_{\text{ev}}$ that @sec-intent-goals-expire takes from the parent belief record.
3. *Dynamic effort invariant:* Requested tool-center-point velocity $v_{\max}$, acceleration $a_{\max}$, and contact wrench $\mathbf{w}_{\max} = [F_{\max}, \tau_{\max}]^\top$ must remain strictly within actuator thermal ratings, link inertia limits, and workpiece structural yield thresholds.
4. *Certified deterministic fallback invariant:* The robot must possess an independently verified, pre-computed stopping or hold trajectory that brings all moving links to rest within current physical obstacle clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clear}}$) if authority is abruptly revoked.

Each invariant addresses a different failure: an uncertain target can exceed the grasp tolerance, old evidence can describe a displaced mug, excessive effort can damage the workpiece, and loss of authority can leave moving mass without a feasible fallback. The intent lease records the target bounds that survive these checks. It constrains the trajectory planner (@sec-planning), which must still construct a motion whose path, timing, and stopping behavior the permission path can admit. @Sec-intent-lease collects the resulting fields after their physical meaning has been established.

The candidate's evidence epoch and finite requested expiry\index{Intent record!temporal lease} make temporal validity enforceable without an asynchronous cancellation message from the proposer. The independent controller checks the admitted deadline and selects a validated hold or stop if the supporting evidence or authority lapses. The deadline mechanism and its drift-derived duration are developed in @sec-intent-goals-expire; here the remaining handoff obligation is to bound the physical effort before that deadline.

A target bounded in space and time remains dangerous if the controller is granted unlimited physical effort. The intent proposal therefore requests explicit effort ceilings\index{Intent record!force limits} on tool-center-point velocity, acceleration, and contact wrench. A goal placed two millimeters inside a rigid workpiece by a small depth error makes a stiff position controller wind up against the surface, driving the actuator toward its current limit and loading the gear train. For the arm's guarded approach to the spring-latched cage door, the proposal requests the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_trip_str` tripwire as its contact-force ceiling, well below the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_lim_str` structural latch limit, and the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_latch_str` approach speed as its velocity cap. The permission path compares each request against independently configured actuator torque-speed limits and task ceilings, admitting only a safe, feasible subset.

Below the permission path, an **impedance controller**\index{Impedance controller}[^fn-impedance-control-hogan] can shape contact loads by regulating the relation between motion and force through a virtual inertia, damping, and stiffness [@hogan1985impedance], the contact model that @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact develops. Under quasi-static contact, the virtual stiffness along the approach axis times the position error gives the steady-state force, so tailoring that stiffness limits the steady load. It does not bound the first impact: approach speed, passive compliance, sensing delay, and actuator response must support the contact limit as well.

[^fn-impedance-control-hogan]: **Impedance Control**\index{Impedance controller!origin}: Hogan's formulation [@hogan1985impedance] regulates neither position nor force alone but the dynamic relation between them, because a manipulator in contact cannot choose both independently: the environment sets one once the controller sets the other. Neither pure position control nor pure force control is safe at a contact whose location is uncertain. The virtual stiffness turns a depth error in the target into a bounded squeeze rather than a controller winding up against its current limit.

Omitting any of these three bounds leaves a physical machine exposed during communication dropouts or perception stalls. Kinetic stopping distance grows linearly with the delay before braking onset and quadratically with physical velocity (@eq-body-stopping-distance). On a mobile base, whose stopping budget is a spatial clearance, a stalled proposer lengthens the delay term by the entire duration its last proposal retains execution authority. That duration is the chunk lease of @sec-nervous-cadences, and it directly inflates the unbraked latency term $\tau_{\text{delay}}$. Under the selected stopping model, the checked obstacle boundary must lie beyond this cumulative stopping distance, including sensor delay and uncertainty margins. The selected powered response also requires drive energy, sensing, and actuator authority to survive the fault; logic hold-up alone cannot supply braking torque.

The intent lease bounds how long the high-level target remains justified. Expiration withdraws permission to keep tracking that target and invokes a validated response. It does not replace the chunk lease or remove sensing, communication, actuator, and braking delays from the stopping budget.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_latch_stall_force_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three orange bars on a log scale against a red dashed vertical line labeled 100 newtons limit. A tripwire bar of 15 newtons and an at-brake bar of 39 newtons end left of the line; a bar for a 200 millisecond stall reaches 2,400 newtons, far past it."}

*A `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_arm_str` unbraked stall drives the latch to `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_unbounded_n_str`, far past its limit.*
:::

::: {#nbk-intent-lease-duration-collision-exposure-tradeoff-across .callout-notebook title="What the latch ceilings buy"}

**Problem**: The intent lease for the cage door requests a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_trip_str` tripwire and a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_latch_str` approach speed against a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_lim_str` latch limit. What happens if the arm's authority to keep pressing outlives the contact loop and waits instead on the proposer?

**Math**: The contact itself is derived in @sec-enforcement-intentional-contact. At this approach speed, @eq-release-trip-indentation carries the force to `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_at_brake_onset_n_str` by the time the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_contact_str` contact-loop response issues the brake command, and the stop that follows has only a fraction of a millimeter of compression left to spend. The lease question is the duration term. If unbraked motion instead continues for `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_arm_str`, a stall shorter than one `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_period_str` intent period, the gripper advances $\Delta x = v_{\text{latch}}\,\Delta t$, or `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.delta_x_unbounded_mm_str`, past first contact, and the plate's linear model gives $F = k_{\text{latch}}\,\Delta x$, or `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_unbounded_n_str`. Meters per second times seconds give meters, and newtons per meter times meters give newtons.

**Systems insight**: The predicted force lies far past the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_lim_str` limit, beyond the point where the spring model applies at all: the latch has failed. The lease therefore does not size the contact stop, which is millisecond work for the contact loop. It carries the two ceilings that make that stop feasible, and it must never leave contact authority waiting on a proposer whose silence is measured in intent periods.
:::

The mug and latch expose different limits on the same **privilege separation boundary**\index{Privilege separation!intent boundary}.[^fn-ai-subsumption-intent] The proposer requests a target and effort bounds; the independent supervisor must retain a feasible response when target evidence expires or contact changes. This separates deliberation from real-time supervision, the layering of early reactive systems with its priority reversed [@brooks1986robust].

[^fn-ai-subsumption-intent]: **Subsumption Architecture**\index{Architecture!subsumption}\index{Control!subsumption}: In the layered controllers of @brooks1986robust, a higher layer subsumes a lower one by suppressing its inputs or inhibiting its outputs. This machine inverts that priority. The lower, real-time layer holds veto authority over the deliberative one, because the lower layer is the one whose timing and failure behavior can be bounded.

The handoff now separates target tolerance, evidence uncertainty, effort, and fallback. The conveyor determines how long those bounds remain useful: even a correctly selected and localized handle moves after capture. Its evidence-growth law supplies the deadline the independent controller must enforce.

## Expiring Goals and Temporal Validity Leases {#sec-intent-goals-expire}

The mug can leave its grasp tolerance while the proposal still names exactly the same coordinate. Target validity therefore needs a deadline derived from physical drift, independent of when the model next produces an output. A temporal lease makes that deadline enforceable even when the proposer stops communicating.

Suppose the application processor hangs while the arm reaches for the red mug. The fault that makes cancellation necessary is the same fault that stops the cancellation from being sent, because an abort needs a working sender, scheduler, and link. An intent lease must therefore expire on its own; this is principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission} applied to a goal. Gray and Cheriton [-@gray1989leases] introduced leases for cache consistency: a coordinator grants time-bounded authority that lapses unless renewed, so a crashed client cannot block others. Their correctness argument holds only while the holder's and the server's clocks drift apart by a bounded amount, which is why the Safety MCU converts every epoch into its own clock with a bounded error. The physical version inverts the stakes. An expired cache lease delays a read; an unexpired motion lease lets moving mass consume clearance. The privileged Safety MCU is therefore the coordinator, granting the unprivileged deliberative layer a transient tracking lease, and when the host stalls, pauses for garbage collection, or panics, the MCU's countdown lapses and it engages its validated fallback without waiting for any packet.[^fn-hw-watchdog-rtt]

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Kinetic momentum budgets and stopping distance constraints originate in @sec-body-kinetic-momentum.
:::

The lease uses the Safety MCU's monotonic hardware clock.[^fn-monotonic-clock-lease] Wall-clock adjustments can change apparent age, and host software callbacks can stall with the process they are meant to supervise. No inference rate, however high, eliminates $P_{99}$ stalls. An independently clocked countdown instead triggers local withdrawal of tracking authority on expiry. This removes host scheduling from expiry detection; it does not remove communication, actuator response, or deceleration from the physical stopping budget.

[^fn-monotonic-clock-lease]: **Monotonic Clock**\index{Clock!monotonic}: A counter that only moves forward at a fixed nominal rate, such as POSIX `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` or a free-running MCU timer. Wall-clock time can be stepped forward or backward by a time-synchronization daemon or an operator, so a lease timed against it can gain or lose its whole remaining window in one adjustment. Every age in this chapter is therefore measured on the MCU's counter and converted from other clocks with a bounded error.

The target-evidence deadline is not new to this chapter. The mug-handle belief record already carries one: its invalidation horizon $T_{\text{inv}}$ (@eq-mem-invalidation-horizon) is the elapsed time at which the record's error growth law (@eq-mem-occlusion-expansion) reaches the task tolerance. The intent lease inherits that horizon as its **target-evidence horizon**\index{Target-evidence horizon} $\tau_{\text{ev}}$, with the grasp tolerance $r_{\text{tol}}$ as the limit $E_{\max}$ and the record's initial error $e_0$ as $E_0$. Here $v_{\text{drift}}$ bounds the relative motion between the gripper frame and the target, including conveyor motion and unmodeled base odometry drift. Two roots of that law govern the conveyor pick. Without tracking, the belt's speed bound drives the error linearly, the case of @eq-mem-linear-horizon with the belt speed as the growth rate $r$. With a tracker that cancels the belt's velocity, only a residual slip acceleration $a_{\text{slip}}$ remains, and the error grows quadratically:
$$\tau_{\text{ev}} = \frac{r_{\text{tol}} - e_0}{v_{\text{drift}}} \quad (a_{\text{slip}} = 0), \qquad \tau_{\text{ev,tracked}} = \sqrt{\frac{2(r_{\text{tol}} - e_0)}{a_{\text{slip}}}} \quad (v_{\text{drift}} = 0)$$ {#eq-intent-evidence-horizon-roots}
When both terms act, the horizon is the positive root of the full quadratic and is shorter than either root alone.

[^fn-hw-watchdog-rtt]: **Watchdog Timer**\index{Hardware!watchdog timer}: An independently clocked down-counter that forces a reset or a safe output unless software reloads it before it reaches zero. A hung host cannot reload it, which is why the lease countdown lives on the MCU and not in the host process it supervises. Detecting the missed renewal is only the first term of the response budget; drive command propagation, brake onset, and deceleration each add a separately measured term.

When $r_{\text{tol}}\le e_0$, the target is inadmissible at capture: sensor uncertainty alone exceeds the task clearance, and the controller immediately refuses dependent motion. Even when the horizon is positive, a separate motion-permission check must verify current clearance against total sensing, permission, communication, and brake-onset delay plus physical braking distance, as in @sec-nervous.

For the red mug on the takeaway conveyor, the grounded target moves at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_conveyor_str`. A `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance and `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str` initial error leave a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` target-evidence horizon by the linear root of @eq-intent-evidence-horizon-roots. Stretching the horizon to the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_period_str` refresh period of the machine's `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_intent_str` intent model would let modeled target error reach `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_at_period_str`, or `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_excess_str` beyond the tolerance. The intent model cannot refresh the target itself, because even a typical inference, at the computed `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_infer_str`, outlasts the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` horizon, and a latency tail only adds to it. Extending the target record to `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_infer_str` solely to hide that delay would leave its estimate outside the declared error envelope for `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_infer_overrun_str`. The `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` limit is an evidence-validity deadline, and only new evidence, checked again against the motion, can extend it; faster compute cannot. Without a qualified tracker the conveyor must slow or pause, or the task must be refused. At `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_drift_slow_str` drift the same bound gives a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_slow_drift_str` evidence horizon (@fig-10-lease-dynamics-tradeoff).

A qualified local tracker changes the arithmetic. It re-measures the mug on every frame and follows the conveyor's velocity, so the conveyor speed no longer drives the error. The same `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str` initial error is still charged against the tolerance, which leaves `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_budget_str` for the residual slip of `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.a_slip_str`, an illustrative worst-case bound, to consume. Against that budget, residual slip alone sets the tracked evidence horizon that @sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline solves, `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str`. The tracker renews that evidence at its own rate, so the tracker's period plus latency is what must fit inside the horizon. The intent model only re-confirms which mug is meant, and each renewal it sends carries the tracker's fresh evidence rather than the frame the model last read. Whichever horizon applies caps the intent lease on this target (@sec-intent-lease).

A host stall shows what each horizon buys. Suppose the arm reaches for the red mug under a target admitted without local tracking, and the application processor stalls in inference. A target held for `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_intent_str` would sit `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_untracked_str` from the physical mug, and the fingers would close on air or strike the rim. The lease does not wait for the host. At `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` it expires, and the arm begins a controlled stop within `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_arm_onset_str` (one permission tick, one fieldbus cycle, and brake onset), while the chunk lease of @sec-nervous-cadences separately bounds active motion. Under the qualified tracker the same `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_intent_str` stall leaves the prediction only `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_tracked_str` off, inside the tolerance, because the tracked horizon runs to `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str`. Local tracking is what makes a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_intent_str` intent rate viable.

@Fig-10-mug-lease-timeline sets both horizons against the intent model's own timing on one clock.

::: {#fig-10-mug-lease-timeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Mug lease against the intent model's timing**: The top lane charges the conveyor mug's modeled target error against the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance. Without tracking, belt speed exhausts it at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str`; with a tracker that cancels belt velocity, residual slip exhausts it at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str`. The bottom lane puts both lease countdowns on the Safety MCU's clock beside the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_infer_str` inference and the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_intent_period_str` proposal period; each expiry is followed by the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_arm_onset_str` stop onset (hatched). Neither lease can wait for the next proposal. After a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_intent_str` host stall the untracked target sits `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_untracked_str` off and the tracked one `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_tracked_str`." fig-alt="Two stacked panels sharing a time axis from 0 to 560 milliseconds. Top: target error in millimeters against time. A dashed bronze line rises from 3 millimeters and crosses a dashed 15-millimeter tolerance line at 60 milliseconds; a solid teal curve crosses it at 219 milliseconds. Square markers at 200 milliseconds mark 43 and 13 millimeters. Bottom: three rows. An intent-model bar ends at 336 milliseconds, with a marker for the next proposal at 500 milliseconds. Two lease bars end at 60 and 219 milliseconds, each followed by a hatched 22-millisecond stop-onset segment."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-intent-mug-lease-timeline
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MUG LEASE AGAINST THE INTENT MODEL'S TIMING (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-10-mug-lease-timeline
# │
# │ Goal:    show why the 2 Hz intent model cannot renew an untracked conveyor
# │          target and what a tracker buys.
# │ Show:    target error vs. time (untracked 60 ms, tracked 219 ms, 15 mm
# │          tolerance, 43/13 mm after a 200 ms stall); lease countdowns with
# │          the 22 ms stop onset beside 336 ms inference and the 500 ms period.
# │ How:     reads calc-intent-lease-duration-collision-exposure; no literals.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, millimeter
from mlsysim.fmt import check

# ┌── 1. LOAD (values from calc-intent-lease-duration-collision-exposure) ─────
E0 = AISLE.grasp_initial_error.to(millimeter).magnitude  # category: illustrative (aisle scenario)
R_TOL = AISLE.grasp_tolerance.to(millimeter).magnitude  # category: illustrative (aisle scenario)
V_BELT = AISLE.v_conveyor.to(millimeter / millisecond).magnitude  # mm per ms
A_SLIP = AISLE.a_conveyor_slip.to(millimeter / millisecond**2).magnitude  # mm per ms^2
T_UNTR = tau_ev_untracked.to(millisecond).magnitude
T_TRK = tau_ev_tracked.to(millisecond).magnitude
T_INFER = RM.intent_inference_latency.to(millisecond).magnitude
T_PERIOD = t_intent_period.to(millisecond).magnitude
T_STALL = delta_t_stall_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude
T_ONSET = t_arm_onset_after_expiry.to(millisecond).magnitude
ERR_STALL_U = err_stalled_untracked.to(millimeter).magnitude
ERR_STALL_T = err_stalled_tracked.to(millimeter).magnitude

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
t = np.linspace(0, 560, 800)
err_untracked = E0 + V_BELT * t
err_tracked = E0 + 0.5 * A_SLIP * t**2
check(abs(np.interp(T_UNTR, t, err_untracked) - R_TOL) < 1e-6, "untracked curve crosses the tolerance at tau_ev")
check(abs(E0 + 0.5 * A_SLIP * T_TRK**2 - R_TOL) < 1e-6, "tracked curve crosses the tolerance at tau_ev,tracked")
Y_TOP = 50.0

# ┌── 3. PLOT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
R = viz.VOL4_ROLES
viz.set_book_style()
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.6, 4.6), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.35, 1.0], "hspace": 0.08})
for a in (ax, bx):
    a.tick_params(labelsize=8.5)
    a.grid(False)
    for s in ("top", "right"):
        a.spines[s].set_visible(False)

# Top lane: modeled target error against the grasp tolerance.
ax.axhspan(R_TOL, Y_TOP, color=R["consequence"], alpha=0.07, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.axhline(R_TOL, color=R["consequence"], lw=1.3, ls=(0, (5, 3)), zorder=2)
ax.text(552, R_TOL + 1.2, f"grasp tolerance $r_{{\\mathrm{{tol}}}}$ = {R_TOL:.0f} mm", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=R["consequence"])
ax.plot(t, np.minimum(err_untracked, Y_TOP + 5), color=R["proposal"], lw=2.0, ls=(0, (6, 2)), zorder=4)
ax.plot(t, np.minimum(err_tracked, Y_TOP + 5), color=R["measured"], lw=2.2, zorder=4)
ax.text(150, 41, "untracked (belt speed)", fontsize=8.5, color=R["proposal"], ha="right", va="center")
ax.text(322, 23, "tracked (residual slip)", fontsize=8.5, color=R["measured"], ha="left", va="center")
# Horizons
for tx, col in ((T_UNTR, R["proposal"]), (T_TRK, R["measured"])):
    ax.plot([tx], [R_TOL], "o", ms=5.5, color=col, zorder=6)
    ax.vlines(tx, 0, R_TOL, color=col, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (1, 2)), zorder=3)
ax.text(T_UNTR + 6, R_TOL - 1.2, f"$\\tau_{{\\mathrm{{ev}}}}$ = {T_UNTR:.0f} ms", fontsize=8.5, color=R["proposal"], ha="left", va="top")
ax.text(T_TRK + 5, 1.2, f"$\\tau_{{\\mathrm{{ev,tracked}}}}$ = {T_TRK:.0f} ms", fontsize=8.5, color=R["measured"], va="bottom")
# Stall points
ax.vlines(T_STALL, 0, Y_TOP, color=R["neutral"], lw=0.8, ls=(0, (3, 3)), zorder=1)
ax.plot([T_STALL], [ERR_STALL_U], "s", ms=5, color=R["proposal"], zorder=6)
ax.plot([T_STALL], [ERR_STALL_T], "s", ms=5, color=R["measured"], zorder=6)
ax.text(
    T_STALL + 6,
    ERR_STALL_U,
    f"{ERR_STALL_U:.0f} mm",
    ha="left",
    va="center",
    fontsize=8.5,
    color=R["proposal"],
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="square,pad=0.08", fc="white", ec="none"),
    zorder=7,
)
ax.annotate(
    f"{ERR_STALL_T:.0f} mm",
    xy=(T_STALL, ERR_STALL_T),
    xytext=(T_STALL - 45, 24),
    ha="center",
    va="center",
    fontsize=8.5,
    color=R["measured"],
    zorder=7,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=R["measured"], lw=0.7, shrinkB=3),
)
ax.text(T_STALL - 5, Y_TOP - 1, f"host stalled {T_STALL:.0f} ms", ha="right", va="top", fontsize=8.5, color=R["neutral"])
ax.set_ylim(0, Y_TOP)
ax.set_yticks([0, E0, R_TOL, 30, 45])
ax.set_ylabel("target error (mm)", fontsize=9)

# Bottom lane: model timing and the two lease countdowns on the MCU clock.
rows = {"intent model": 2.0, "untracked lease": 1.0, "tracked lease": 0.0}
H = 0.5

def tint(hex_color, a):
    h = hex_color.lstrip("#")
    return tuple(1 - a * (1 - int(h[i : i + 2], 16) / 255) for i in (0, 2, 4))

bx.broken_barh([(0, T_INFER)], (rows["intent model"] - H / 2, H), facecolor=tint(R["proposal"], 0.22), edgecolor=R["proposal"], lw=1.0)
bx.text(T_INFER / 2, rows["intent model"], f"inference {T_INFER:.0f} ms", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color="#1A202C")
bx.plot([T_PERIOD], [rows["intent model"]], marker="v", ms=6.5, color=R["proposal"], zorder=5)
bx.text(T_PERIOD - 9, rows["intent model"], f"next proposal {T_PERIOD:.0f} ms", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=R["proposal"])
for name, tx in (("untracked lease", T_UNTR), ("tracked lease", T_TRK)):
    y = rows[name]
    bx.broken_barh([(0, tx)], (y - H / 2, H), facecolor=tint(R["structural"], 0.18), edgecolor=R["structural"], lw=1.0)
    bx.broken_barh([(tx, T_ONSET)], (y - H / 2, H), facecolor=tint(R["consequence"], 0.15), edgecolor=R["consequence"], lw=1.0, hatch="////")
    bx.plot([tx, tx], [y - H / 2 - 0.08, y + H / 2 + 0.08], color=R["consequence"], lw=1.6)
    bx.text(tx + T_ONSET + 8, y, f"expiry {tx:.0f} ms, stop onset +{T_ONSET:.0f} ms", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color="#1A202C")
bx.set_yticks(list(rows.values()))
bx.set_yticklabels(list(rows.keys()), fontsize=8.5)
bx.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
bx.set_ylim(-0.55, 2.55)
bx.set_xlim(0, 560)
bx.set_xlabel("time since capture (ms)", fontsize=9)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.17, right=0.98, top=0.98, bottom=0.11)
plt.show()
```

Continuous tracking requires *fresh physical evidence*, not merely a new packet from the same stale frame. A renewal based on a new capture must arrive before the current evidence and admitted authority expire, with capture, processing, transfer, clock uncertainty, and permission time included in its budget. The simple condition $T_{\text{period}}+t_{\text{latency}}<\tau_{\text{ev}}$ is only a necessary scheduling check. When a fresh proposal arrives, the planner may compute a jerk-limited splice\index{Trajectory Generation!jerk-limited splice} from the measured state. It admits that splice only if the swept path, new evidence, and stopping reserve remain feasible; an abrupt target change can instead require refusal or a checked stop.

When the countdown the MCU armed at admission runs out, whether or not the host is still running, the independent controller withdraws the proposal's authority and selects a previously validated response\index{Safety!deterministic terminal state} for the measured load and contact mode. An active position hold needs torque and can protect a suspended payload; controlled deceleration needs brake capability and clearance; torque disable can be suitable for some drives but can release a load or leave momentum uncontrolled. The proposer may request a mode, but it cannot choose the terminal action for the MCU. Admission fails when no response remains feasible from the current state.

Executing an expiring lease safely assumes that the commanded geometric proposal is actually achievable by the physical body. If a proposed coordinate lies beyond kinematic reach\index{Kinematics!workspace reachability} or demands joint velocities that exceed actuator limits\index{Actuator!velocity limits} during the lease window, granting the lease wastes control authority and can trip the drive's overcurrent protection as a motor draws excessive current toward an impossible speed. Determining whether a goal is kinematically and dynamically admissible belongs before the trajectory generator accepts the lease, establishing a physical filter between high-level intent and motion execution.

## Admissible Goal Sets {#sec-intent-admissible-goal-sets}

If the red mug rides past on the far side of the belt, beyond the arm's physical reach from where the base is parked, no sequence of joint torques can bring the gripper to its handle. In an embodied ML system, this physical impossibility must be intercepted at the proposal boundary\index{Proposal boundary!goal filtering}, before the target enters the trajectory optimization queue. When an upstream vision-language model\index{Vision-language model} or diffusion policy emits a candidate Cartesian coordinate, treating that proposal as an unverified candidate protects the real-time motion pipeline from executing impossible trajectories, and even from attempting to solve them.

A reachability screen also protects the planner's compute budget. If a target cannot be reached at all, the trajectory optimizer of @sec-planning faces an empty feasible set, and a local nonlinear solver cannot certify that emptiness quickly: it typically spends its whole iteration budget before timing out, turning a geometric hallucination upstream into compute starvation on the planning core. A requested terminal move that cannot finish before its supporting evidence expires should likewise fail before detailed planning. A longer task can instead request guarded progress under renewable evidence; that is a different request from completing the grasp on one capture.

To avoid spending the planning budget on an already impossible request, the admission layer first applies two lower-cost checks. Their execution and evidence-query budgets still require qualification:

1. **Static Workspace Manifold Check ($\mathbf{T}_{\text{target}} \in \mathcal{W}$):** Geometric workspace analysis defines the closed spatial manifold $\mathcal{W} \subset SE(3)$ of reachable end-effector configurations given link dimensions, joint travel limits, and mounting geometry [@craig2005introduction; @lynch2017modern].[^fn-math-workspace-manifold] An analytical reachability check evaluates whether the target $SE(3)$\index{SE(3)} pose $\mathbf{T}_{\text{target}}$ resides inside this workspace manifold $\mathcal{W}$, while an occupancy lookup in spatial memory confirms that the target volume does not intersect persistent static obstacles.
2. **Dynamic Reachability Transit Check:** For a terminal move supported by one evidence record, even if a target lies inside the static workspace manifold $\mathcal{W}$, it may be physically unreachable within the finite window during which its sensor evidence remains valid. **Dynamic reachability**\index{Dynamic reachability} is the condition that the end effector can transition from its measured state $(\mathbf{p}_0, \mathbf{v}_0)$ to the target pose within the remaining window $t_{\text{intent\_exp}} - t_{\text{now}}$ while respecting its velocity, acceleration, jerk, and thermal torque limits.

Whatever continuous trajectory profile the actuators follow, no physical move covers distance $d = \|\mathbf{p}_{\text{target}} - \mathbf{p}_0\|$ faster than its maximum speed ceiling allows. Here both $\mathbf{p}$ terms are translation vectors in the same Cartesian frame, not full $SE(3)$ poses; orientation feasibility requires a separate check. For terminal completion before the current expiry, a necessary condition is:
$$\frac{d}{v_{\max}} \le t_{\text{intent\_exp}} - t_{\text{now}}.$$ {#eq-intent-dynamic-reachability-bound}
Actuator acceleration limits, jerk ceilings, and motor torque-speed curves only lengthen the required transit time. A proposal that violates this inequality cannot promise terminal completion in that window. A request for an intermediate guarded segment may remain feasible if its executed motion and fallback fit the current authority and its continuation requires newly admitted evidence. @Sec-appendix-control-reachability derives triangular and trapezoidal transit bounds and explains how jerk limits change the complete-move check.

The scalar lower bound is an early rejection test, not a path solver. It avoids optimizing a terminal request that is already too late, while leaving acceleration, obstacles, and stopping reserve to the fuller motion check. No rejection fraction or execution-time bound follows from the inequality alone.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Admissible goal regions specify the boundary conditions for spline generation in @sec-planning-continuous-trajectories.
:::

[^fn-math-workspace-manifold]: **Workspace Versus Singularity**\index{Kinematics!workspace boundaries}: Membership in $\mathcal{W}$ says that some joint configuration reaches the pose, not that the arm can move freely there; inside the workspace the Jacobian can still lose rank at a singular configuration, where some Cartesian velocities become unattainable. A workspace screen therefore rejects unreachable targets but leaves singularities to the configuration and path checks of @sec-appendix-control-kinematics.

On the arm, the mug's evidence under the qualified tracker stays valid for `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str` after its capture. At the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_tcp_str` tool center point (TCP) speed limit, the gripper could cover at most `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_reach_tracked_str` even if the entire window remained. A terminal proposal issued with the gripper `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_target_str` from the handle needs at least `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_transit_floor_str` of transit. It therefore receives `ERR_DYNAMIC_TIME_INSUFFICIENT` if it promises completion on that record. Without the tracker, the full window is only `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` and the corresponding speed-only reach is `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_reach_untracked_str`. Processing and transport consume part of either window; acceleration further reduces the reachable distance.

This bound and the fuller checks behind it assume that actuators stay within their nominal thermal ratings, that encoders report the initial state $(\mathbf{p}_0, \mathbf{v}_0)$ correctly, and that the payload matches the inertial model. When winding temperatures cross the thresholds of @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles, or a force measurement shows a payload mismatch, the permission path lowers $a_{\max}$ and $v_{\max}$ (**thermal derating**\index{Thermal derating}), evaluates new proposals against the reduced limits, and rechecks any admitted path that the derating may have made infeasible.

A rejection must not simply discard the packet, which would leave the reasoning model waiting for a task timeout. The intent filter returns a structured diagnostic across the proposal boundary: the classification (`ERR_WORKSPACE_OUT_OF_BOUNDS`, `ERR_DYNAMIC_TIME_INSUFFICIENT`, or `ERR_OCCUPANCY_BLOCKED`) and the numerical margin of failure. A dynamic failure reports the shortfall between the transit bound and the remaining window; a workspace failure reports the nearest reachable point on the boundary of $\mathcal{W}$. The reasoning layer can then seek fresher evidence, choose another approach, slow the process, or propose moving the base. It cannot extend the evidence horizon without new evidence.

The diagnostic makes a staged approach possible. Stipulate, as conditions of the example rather than test results, that the pre-contact corridor and its stopping reserve are qualified, that a closer wrist observation supports the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str` error bound, and that the tracker holds the declared slip bound. The rejected terminal promise becomes a pre-contact observation goal: a separately checked corridor carries the gripper toward a better view while keeping a stop outside contact, and the closer capture supplies the mug-handle belief record whose error fits the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` tolerance.

Better sensing does not shorten the physical transit floor. The `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_target_str` approach still takes at least `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_transit_floor_str`, longer than the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str` horizon of any one capture, so it needs at least `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.n_captures_str` fresh captures. The planner executes guarded segments under the chunk leases of @sec-nervous-cadences, and each continuation is checked against the current intent, target evidence, corridor, and fallback; the predicted route beyond the admitted segment carries no authority. Once the last segment and the closure pass the full trajectory check, the gripper completes the grasp inside the tolerance and moves to the admitted hold for handover. If the closer observation fails, identity becomes unresolved, or a renewal arrives late, the next segment is refused, and existing motion continues only while its own evidence, authority, and fallback remain valid. @Sec-planning constructs the timed segments and their continuations.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_dynamic_reachability_shortfall_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Horizontal bar labeled transit floor, 300 milliseconds, runs past a red dashed line labeled evidence 219 milliseconds into a shaded region beyond it. Text below reads needs 2 captures."}

*The `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_transit_floor_str` reach outlasts one `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str` evidence window; it needs `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.n_captures_str` captures.*
:::

### Dynamic obstacle forecasting and forward occupancy {#sec-intent-dynamic-forecasting}

A mug may be reachable while a coworker is about to cross the approach corridor. The workspace and transit tests alone cannot reject that conflict. **Dynamic obstacle forecasting**\index{Dynamic obstacle!forward occupancy forecasting} carries the perception and memory estimates forward into regions that moving obstacles could occupy. At the intent stage, these regions support early corridor rejection; the planner and permission path must later check the complete timed trajectory.

The intent filter consumes the dynamic track manifest $[(\text{ID}_k, \hat{\mathbf{p}}_k, \hat{\mathbf{v}}_k, \mathbf{P}_k, t_{\text{last}}, \text{state})]$ published by the multi-object tracker (@sec-perception-tracking-association), alongside tentative detections, raw occupied regions, and unknown-space evidence: failure to confirm an identity does not make its occupied region clear. For each confirmed or coasting track $k$, the admission engine constructs a **forward occupancy set**\index{Forward occupancy set} $\mathcal{R}_k(\Delta t)$, the region the actor could occupy $\Delta t$ after its last measurement:
$$\mathcal{R}_k(\Delta t) = \left\{ \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \;\middle|\; \|\mathbf{p} - \hat{\mathbf{p}}_k\| \le r_k + v_h \Delta t + k_\sigma \sigma_{\text{track}}(\Delta t) \right\}$$ {#eq-intent-forward-occupancy}
Here $r_k$ is a declared body envelope that covers torso, limbs, and carried objects; $v_h$ is a validated bound on the actor's speed; $k_\sigma$ is a selected multiplier whose joint spatial coverage must be calibrated rather than read off a scalar Gaussian rule; and $\sigma_{\text{track}}(\Delta t)$ is the root-mean-square position deviation of the propagated track covariance. That deviation need not grow monotonically during coasting, so the check needs a conservative bound over the whole interval. The set is named for occupancy rather than reach so that it is not confused with the arm's dynamic reachability defined earlier in this section: one asks where the robot can get in time, the other where a person might be. A tracker with a validated acceleration bound can instead center the set on the predicted position $\hat{\mathbf{p}}_k + \hat{\mathbf{v}}_k \Delta t$ and grow it with $\frac{1}{2} a_{k,\max} \Delta t^2$, which is tighter over short intervals; the speed-bound form is the conservative one that safety standards use.

@Eq-intent-forward-occupancy is the human half of **speed and separation monitoring**\index{Speed and separation monitoring} (SSM). ISO 10218-2:2025, which incorporates the collaborative-application requirements formerly published as ISO/TS 15066 (the technical specification itself remains published and is under revision), sizes a protective separation distance from the person's travel over the robot's reaction and stopping time, the robot's own travel and stopping distance, and the position uncertainty of both, and ISO 13855 supplies the walking approach speed[^fn-approach-speed-constant] of `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_h_str` that such calculations assume for an approaching person [@iso10218part2; @isots15066; @iso13855; @marvel2017implementing]. @Sec-body-stopping-distance-prebrake maps those terms onto the machine's stopping budget. The intent stage uses the same speed bound for an earlier and coarser purpose, rejecting a corridor before the planner spends time on it.

[^fn-approach-speed-constant]: **Approach-Speed Constant**\index{ISO 13855!approach speed}: The standard's speed describes a design person walking toward a safeguard, not a measured coworker, and the standard applies a higher constant to hand and arm reach at short separations [@iso13855]. A forecast built on the walking value is valid only for the motion it describes. A coworker who runs or reaches across the corridor lies outside that bound, which is why the growth term must be validated for the site rather than copied from the standard.

A candidate transit corridor $\mathcal{T}_{\text{robot}}(\Delta t)$ can be screened against each actor's set (@fig-10-dynamic-reachability-cones). The geometric condition in @eq-intent-dynamic-exclusion becomes a full trajectory requirement only after the planner supplies the machine's swept volume over time. Under the declared obstacle-motion and uncertainty bounds, that volume must avoid every occupancy set throughout the proposed execution window:
$$\mathcal{T}_{\text{robot}}(\Delta t) \cap \mathcal{R}_k(\Delta t) = \emptyset \quad \forall \Delta t \in [0, t_{\text{intent\_exp}} - t_{\text{now}}], \;\; \forall k$$ {#eq-intent-dynamic-exclusion}
If a candidate corridor intersects an expanding set, the early screen can return `ERR_DYNAMIC_OCCUPANCY_CONFLICT` and request a different corridor or a yield. The refusal diagnostic returns the earliest predicted conflict time $\Delta t_{\text{conflict}}$ and the conflicting actor identifier $\text{ID}_k$. Passing this screen does not establish a collision-free trajectory: the planner must supply the timed motion, and the permission path must check its swept volume and stopping reserve against evidence that remains valid.

On the machine the growth term is easy to size. Over the mug's `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str` tracked evidence horizon, a coworker at the ISO 13855 speed can move `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_occ_tracked_str`. Over a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_forecast_long_str` planning horizon the same term reaches `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_occ_long_str`, more than twice the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.aisle_width_str` aisle width, so one person's set blocks the aisle. That is the root of the **freezing robot problem**\index{Freezing robot problem}. Trautman and Krause showed that when a planner predicts each person independently and lets that uncertainty grow, the predicted occupancy of a crowd covers every path, and the robot stops even though people would make room for it [@trautman2010unfreezing]. Three choices reduce unnecessary conservatism, and none permits shrinking a physically justified bound merely to obtain motion:

1. *Short receding horizons:* Screening over the evidence horizon rather than seconds ahead keeps the growth term near `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_occ_tracked_str` instead of meters. The forecast must still cover the entire executed prefix and the physical fallback, including response delay and deceleration; shortening the lease does not shorten an actor's possible motion while the robot stops.
2. *Re-centering on fresh evidence:* A qualified tracker re-centers each set on new measurements ($t_0 \leftarrow t_{\text{fresh}}$), resetting the growth term and the propagated covariance, provided its accuracy and latency support the required bound.
3. *Interaction-aware prediction:* Trautman and Krause's own remedy predicts the people and the robot jointly, so that each accounts for how the others will respond. Such predictions are learned or modeled proposals, and they may narrow a set only after their error has been bounded by the same kind of evidence the permission path demands of any other input.

::: {#fig-10-dynamic-reachability-cones fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Forward occupancy sets on the aisle**: A top-down view of a candidate corridor screened against a coworker's forward occupancy sets, centered on the last measured position. The discs show only the growth term $v_h\Delta t$ at the ISO 13855 speed of `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_h_str`: `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_occ_untracked_str` over the untracked `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str` horizon and `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_occ_tracked_str` over the tracked `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str` horizon; the body envelope $r_k$ and the tracking term $k_\sigma\sigma_{\text{track}}$ add to every radius. The corridor enters the tracked set (red segment), so the screen refuses it and asks for a detour or yield. Over a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_forecast_long_str` horizon the set grows to `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.d_occ_long_str` and spans the aisle." fig-alt="Top-down view of a horizontal aisle between two racks, with a gap in the lower rack for a cross aisle. A robot on the left has a straight path to a goal on the right. A coworker dot near the lower rack sits inside a small dashed disc labeled 96 millimeters at 60 milliseconds and a larger disc labeled 351 millimeters at 219 milliseconds. The path segment inside the larger disc is red and labeled as where the corridor enters the tracked set. A pale wash fills the aisle, labeled as the 3.2-meter set at 2 seconds spanning the aisle."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-intent-reachability-sets
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FORWARD OCCUPANCY SETS ON THE AISLE (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-10-dynamic-reachability-cones
# │
# │ Goal:    show the corridor screen against a coworker's growing set, and
# │          why a multi-second horizon freezes the robot.
# │ Show:    growth term v_h*dt at 1.6 m/s: 96 mm at 60 ms, 351 mm at 219 ms,
# │          3.2 m at 2 s against the 1.3 m aisle.
# │ How:     reads calc-intent-lease-duration-collision-exposure; the scene
# │          positions are drawing choices, declared below.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Rectangle
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, millimeter, meter
from mlsysim.fmt import check

# ┌── 1. LOAD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
V_H = AISLE.v_human_approach.to(meter / ureg.second).magnitude  # ISO 13855 walking speed
W_AISLE = AISLE.aisle_width.to(meter).magnitude
T_UNTR = tau_ev_untracked.to(ureg.second).magnitude
T_TRK = tau_ev_tracked.to(ureg.second).magnitude
T_LONG = t_forecast_long.to(ureg.second).magnitude
# Scene geometry for the drawing only (not a physical claim):
P_ACTOR = np.array([3.0, 0.35])  # m, coworker's last measured position  # category: illustrative (drawing)
Y_PATH = W_AISLE / 2  # m, candidate corridor centerline  # category: illustrative (drawing)
X_ROBOT, X_GOAL = 0.35, 5.6  # m  # category: illustrative (drawing)
RACK = 0.45  # m, drawn rack depth  # category: illustrative (drawing)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: growth term v_h * dt of the forward occupancy set ──────────
radii = {dt: V_H * dt for dt in (T_UNTR, T_TRK, T_LONG)}
gap = abs(Y_PATH - P_ACTOR[1])  # actor-to-centerline distance
r_trk = radii[T_TRK]
half_chord = np.sqrt(max(r_trk**2 - gap**2, 0.0))
check(radii[T_UNTR] < gap < r_trk, "drawn corridor clears the 60 ms set and meets the 219 ms set")
check(radii[T_LONG] > 2 * W_AISLE, "2 s set spans more than twice the aisle width")

# ┌── 3. PLOT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
viz.set_book_style()
C = viz.COLORS
R = viz.VOL4_ROLES
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.1))
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.grid(False)
ax.set_xlim(-0.1, 6.1)
ax.set_ylim(-RACK - 0.15, W_AISLE + RACK + 0.15)
for s in ax.spines.values():
    s.set_visible(False)
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_yticks([])

# Racks (cross aisle opening in the south rack under the coworker)
gap_x = (2.5, 3.5)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((-0.1, W_AISLE), 6.2, RACK, facecolor="#EDEDED", edgecolor="#9A9A9A", lw=0.8, zorder=1))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((-0.1, -RACK), gap_x[0] + 0.1, RACK, facecolor="#EDEDED", edgecolor="#9A9A9A", lw=0.8, zorder=1))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((gap_x[1], -RACK), 6.1 - gap_x[1], RACK, facecolor="#EDEDED", edgecolor="#9A9A9A", lw=0.8, zorder=1))
ax.text(0.0, W_AISLE + RACK / 2, "rack", fontsize=8.5, color="#6B6B6B", va="center")
ax.text(0.0, -RACK / 2, "rack", fontsize=8.5, color="#6B6B6B", va="center")
ax.text(np.mean(gap_x), -RACK + 0.05, "cross aisle", fontsize=8.5, color="#6B6B6B", ha="center", va="center")

# The 2 s set: its boundary lies outside the drawn aisle segment on both sides.
_wash = ax.add_patch(Circle(P_ACTOR, radii[T_LONG], facecolor=R["measured"], alpha=0.08, edgecolor="none", zorder=2))
_floor = Rectangle((-0.1, 0.0), 6.2, W_AISLE, transform=ax.transData)
_wash.set_clip_path(_floor)
# Nested sets over the two evidence horizons
ax.add_patch(Circle(P_ACTOR, r_trk, facecolor="#E6F2F3", edgecolor=R["measured"], lw=1.3, zorder=3))
ax.add_patch(Circle(P_ACTOR, radii[T_UNTR], facecolor="#DCEEF0", edgecolor=R["measured"], lw=1.1, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=4))
ax.plot(*P_ACTOR, marker="o", ms=6, color=R["measured"], zorder=6)
ax.text(P_ACTOR[0] + r_trk + 0.08, P_ACTOR[1] - 0.05, "coworker, last measured", fontsize=8.5, color=R["measured"], va="center", ha="left", zorder=6)

# Radius callouts
ax.annotate("", xy=(P_ACTOR[0] - r_trk, P_ACTOR[1]), xytext=P_ACTOR, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=R["measured"], lw=0.9), zorder=6)
ax.text(
    P_ACTOR[0] - r_trk - 0.06,
    P_ACTOR[1] - 0.02,
    f"{r_trk * 1000:.0f} mm\nat {T_TRK * 1000:.0f} ms",
    fontsize=8.5,
    color=R["measured"],
    ha="right",
    va="center",
    zorder=6,
)

# Candidate corridor centerline: admitted prefix, conflict segment, remainder
x0, x1 = P_ACTOR[0] - half_chord, P_ACTOR[0] + half_chord
ax.plot([X_ROBOT, x0], [Y_PATH, Y_PATH], color=R["proposal"], lw=2.0, zorder=5)
ax.plot([x0, x1], [Y_PATH, Y_PATH], color=R["consequence"], lw=3.2, zorder=5)
ax.annotate("", xy=(X_GOAL, Y_PATH), xytext=(x1, Y_PATH), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=R["proposal"], lw=2.0, ls=(0, (4, 2))), zorder=5)
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((X_ROBOT - 0.25, Y_PATH - 0.2), 0.3, 0.4, facecolor="#FFFFFF", edgecolor="#333333", lw=1.2, zorder=6))
ax.text(X_ROBOT - 0.1, Y_PATH + 0.28, "robot", fontsize=8.5, ha="center", va="bottom", zorder=6)
ax.text(X_GOAL, Y_PATH + 0.1, "goal", fontsize=8.5, ha="center", va="bottom", zorder=6)
ax.text(
    P_ACTOR[0],
    Y_PATH + 0.1,
    "corridor enters the tracked set",
    fontsize=8.5,
    color=R["consequence"],
    ha="center",

    zorder=7,

)
ax.text(
    4.35,
    W_AISLE - 0.1,
    f"{radii[T_LONG]:.1f} m set at {T_LONG:.0f} s spans the aisle",
    fontsize=8.5,
    color=R["measured"],
    ha="center",
    va="top",
    zorder=6,
)
ax.annotate(
    f"{radii[T_UNTR] * 1000:.0f} mm at {T_UNTR * 1000:.0f} ms",

    xytext=(P_ACTOR[0], -0.1),
```
